notes.meaning: The Levites were the temple helpers who served alongside the priests. Six Levites are named here, all of whom had married foreign wives. They seem to come from the Levite families listed in Ezra 2:40. Kelita, the man's usual name, and Jozabad both show up again later in Nehemiah 8:7.

Next come one temple singer and three gatekeepers, the men who guarded the temple doors. They were counted as Levites too, so ten Levites are named in all. Even the men who led worship in song were held to account. This shows how thorough the clean-up was.

"Other Israelites" means the ordinary people, set apart from the priests and Levites named before. So turning back to God was not only for religious leaders. Plain families were held to account too. The family of Parosh is named first, and men from this same family later helped rebuild Jerusalem's walls (Nehemiah 3:25).

These six men came from the family of Elam. Shechaniah, the man who first urged the people to make a covenant (a solemn promise to God) in 10:2, was also from Elam. He seems not to have married a foreign wife himself. But his own father and uncles seem to be on this list, and he still stood with the guilty.

Six men from the family of Zattu are named. Like the other families in this list, Zattu's family was among those who came back from exile in Babylon (Ezra 2). Many of these names appear again in Nehemiah. But we cannot be sure they are the same men.

Four men from the family of Bebai are named. We know nothing more about these men than what is written here. Matthew Henry says their names were written down to their shame. Yet they also stand as men who owned their sin and turned from it.
Six men from the family of Bani are named. Oddly, Bani is named again in verse 34. One of the two places is likely a copying slip for another family name, most likely the second one.

Eight men came from the family of Pahath-moab, another family that had come home from Babylon. Compared with all the people who had returned, the guilty were few. But many were leading men, and their example could easily have spread the problem.

Eight men from the family of Harim are listed. The writer gives the names one by one, in full. Some point out that he spends two whole chapters on this matter, which shows how seriously the Bible treats it.

Seven men from the family of Hashum are named. Matthew Henry thinks each man was given a fair hearing before Ezra and the leaders. He also thinks a wife who had truly turned to Israel's God was not sent away. Weighing each case would have needed great care.

A long group begins here, said to be from the family of Bani. Other families have four to eight names each, but this group has twenty-seven. Ezra 10:7 and 14 say men from other towns in Judah were also involved. So these men may have come from several towns, not from one family.
The list of this large group goes on. Ezra and the leaders worked hard and steadily. They finished every case in about three months.
These names are listed under Binnui. They belong to the same long group of twenty-seven men begun in verse 34. These men, too, may have come from towns around Judah.
The long group ends with these names. Matthew Henry reminds us that even the best reformers can only do their best. Only the Redeemer, when He comes, will fully turn God's people away from sin.

The family of Nebo closes the list with seven names. In all, about 113 men are named: 17 priests, 10 Levites and 86 ordinary Israelites. One writer gives a picture: you can pull out the nails, but the holes remain. Sin can be put away, yet its marks are left behind.

The account ends by saying all these men had married foreign women, and some had children by them. Older commentators take this to mean only a few had children, and some see God's hand in making the parting less hard. It also shows how fully the reform was carried out, since leaving a wife who is a mother is far harder. Matthew Henry thinks the children were probably not sent away and the wives were cared for. He notes the problem came back later (Nehemiah 13), because only Christ can truly take sin away.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many scholars say the Hebrew of this verse is hard to read and may have been damaged in copying. Some translations, such as the NRSV and Good News, follow another old reading: they sent away the wives along with their children.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars read Ezra 9–10 as building up a sense of separation between the returned exiles and the "people of the land." They say the two groups were once one people. They also point out that many other Old Testament passages do not object to such marriages the way Ezra does.
